map_panel <- function(col, label, palette) {
  ggplot(eu_sf) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[col]]), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    coord_sf(xlim = eu_bbox[c("xmin", "xmax")],
             ylim = eu_bbox[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
    # direction = 1 because distiller defaults to -1, which would paint low
    # values dark and silently invert every panel against the leaflet map.
    scale_fill_distiller(palette = palette, direction = 1, na.value = "grey90",
                         labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
    labs(title = label, fill = NULL) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(
      plot.title        = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 4)),
      # without the bottom margin the row-1 colourbars land on the row-2 titles
      # and the row-2 colourbars get clipped by the figure edge.
      plot.margin       = margin(4, 6, 14, 6),
      legend.position   = "bottom",
      legend.margin     = margin(t = 6, b = 0),
      legend.text       = element_text(size = 7),
      legend.key.height = unit(3, "pt"),
      legend.key.width  = unit(28, "pt")
    )
}

wrap_plots(pmap(metrics, map_panel), nrow = 2, ncol = 3) +
  plot_annotation(title = paste(map_education, "-", map_age_group))

section: Master’s over Doctorate: the same six metrics
text:
Master’s over Doctorate: the same six metrics
The grid above fixes education, so it cannot show what the education level does to each measure. Here the six metrics are the columns and the two education levels are the rows: read down a column to compare Master’s against Doctorate, across a row to compare measures within one level.


Show the code
edu_slice <- function(edu) {
  s <- borders |>
    left_join(filter(data_wide, education == edu, age_group == map_age_group),
              by = c("ISO3_CODE" = "iso3"))
  stopifnot(nrow(s) == nrow(borders))   # one row, one geometry, one country
  s
}

sf_mas <- edu_slice("Master's")
sf_phd <- edu_slice("Doctorate")

# Fail if a metric ever goes empty in both slices: `range()`
stopifnot(all(metrics$col %in% names(sf_phd)),
          !sapply(metrics$col, \(c) all(is.na(c(sf_mas[[c]], sf_phd[[c]])))))

# One gradient per metric. All six are ColorBrewer sequential ramps, so each is
# still colour-blind safe on its own. Purples and PuRd are the closest pair of
# the six, which is why they are not neighbouring columns; Greys is left out
# because grey90 below already means "no data". Local to this figure --
# `metrics$palette` still drives the 6-panel grid and the leaflet map.
edu_palettes <- c(
  pct_happy              = "PuRd",
  pct_satisfied_finances = "Blues",
  pct_satisfied_leisure  = "Greens",
  pct_permanent_contract = "Purples",
  earnings_gross_yearly  = "YlOrBr",
  hours_worked           = "OrRd"
)
stopifnot(setequal(names(edu_palettes), metrics$col))

# Per metric, not per panel: both rows of a column read off the same scale.
edu_limits <- setNames(
  lapply(metrics$col, \(col) range(c(sf_mas[[col]], sf_phd[[col]]), na.rm = TRUE)),
  metrics$col
)

# Map function
map_panel_edu <- function(sf_slice, col, palette, limits, title, subtitle) {
  ggplot(sf_slice) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[col]]), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    coord_sf(xlim = eu_bbox[c("xmin", "xmax")],
             ylim = eu_bbox[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_distiller(palette = palette, direction = 1, limits = limits,
                         na.value = "grey90",
                         labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, fill = NULL) +
    theme_void(base_size = 8) +
    theme(
      plot.title        = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 1)),
      plot.subtitle     = element_text(size = 7, hjust = 0, colour = "grey30",
                                       margin = margin(b = 4)),
      plot.margin       = margin(4, 4, 12, 4),
      legend.position   = "bottom",
      legend.text       = element_text(size = 6),
      legend.key.height = unit(3, "pt"),
      legend.key.width  = unit(20, "pt")
    )
}


edu_row <- function(sf_slice, edu) {
  pmap(metrics, function(col, label, ...)    # gradient comes from edu_palettes
    map_panel_edu(sf_slice, col, edu_palettes[[col]], edu_limits[[col]],
                  label, edu))
}

wrap_plots(c(edu_row(sf_mas, "Master's"), edu_row(sf_phd, "Doctorate")),
           nrow = 2, ncol = 6) +
  plot_annotation(title = paste("Master's over Doctorate -", map_age_group))

text:
Two metrics side by side
Do any of these metrics actually correlate?
With the ShinyMap bellow, you can select any two of the metrics, and it will return there corresponding maps and there correlation scores, for both education level simultaneously.
The interactivity we had above is not enough to let us do that.
We need our new shinyMap.R kept out of the .qmd to avoid rendering issues.
The app draws the same data_wide slices and reuses the leaflet recipe from add_metric_layer() above — colorNumeric() fill, no data labels for the 4-6 countries missing per measure, the same CartoDB.PositronNoLabels tiles and the same fixed eu_bbox.
What you can do: 1. Select two metrics 2. Visualize the correlation directly 3. Click any country on the maps or on the scatter plots. 4. Deepen your request by selecting age categories.
Each scatter reports its own Pearson and Spearman correlation with the n it was computed from, and a toggle puts both rows of a column on one shared colour scale — the edu_limits trick from the twelve-map grid, without which the darkest shade means something different in the Master’s map than in the Doctorate one.


Show the code
# From the project root. eval: false above -- this never runs during a render.
# This is the fast path while developing: real R, instant reload.
shiny::runApp("shinyMap.R")



Getting it into this page: R compiled to WebAssembly
The chunk above needs a live R process, which a rendered .html does not have. To make the app work in this page the R process has to move into the reader’s browser, and that is what shinylive does: it ships webR – R itself compiled to WebAssembly – alongside wasm builds of every package the app loads. No server, no shinyapps.io account, and the result is still a static site.
Every package this app needs is available as a wasm binary from repo.r-wasm.org: shiny, bslib, dplyr, readr, sf, leaflet and plotly.
We just needed to save the borders file into a file locally.


Show the code
# 2 decimal places is ~1 km at these latitudes, invisible at 1:20 million, and
# it takes the file from 156 KB to 137 KB. Only the two columns the app uses.
sf::st_write(
  dplyr::select(borders, ISO3_CODE, NAME_ENGL),
  "borders.geojson",
  driver        = "GeoJSON",
  delete_dsn    = TRUE,
  quiet         = TRUE,
  layer_options = "COORDINATE_PRECISION=2"
)


So the export lives in export_shinylive.R and runs as a pre-render step, declared in _quarto.yml alongside the resources: entry it has to precede. It downloads webR and a wasm binary for every package the app loads, so the first build takes minutes; shinylive caches them afterwards. Pre-render scripts are not covered by freeze: auto and would otherwise re-export on every single render, so the script skips the work unless shinyMap.R is newer than the bundle. Delete shinylive_app/ to force a rebuild after a data change.

title: Find Your Best Match
text:
The Personalised Country Wellbeing Score (PCWS) is an interactive country recommendation tool based on OECD wellbeing data. Rather than identifying one country as universally “best”, the model evaluates countries according to a user’s demographic profile and the aspects of wellbeing that matter most to that individual.
The user provides:
These inputs are combined with OECD indicators to produce a personalised score for each country and a ranked recommendation.

library(shiny)

#Loading data
#The CSV is embedded directly in this Shinylive application.
#This means the browser app does not depend on the user's working directory.
df <- read.csv(
  "data_wide.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

#Making sure data is numeric
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    pct_happy = as.numeric(pct_happy),
    pct_satisfied_finances = as.numeric(pct_satisfied_finances),
    pct_satisfied_leisure = as.numeric(pct_satisfied_leisure),
    pct_permanent_contract = as.numeric(pct_permanent_contract),
    earnings_gross_yearly = as.numeric(earnings_gross_yearly),
    hours_worked = as.numeric(hours_worked)
  )

#Making the functions for compatability
#Transforming the values so that they match the other indicators % style on a scale of 0-100

#Income compatability
income_match <- function(country_income, desired_income) {

  difference <- abs(country_income - desired_income)

  # Exponential, No difference → score of 100. Bigger difference → rapidly smaller score.
  #"Small differences are meaningful, but once two things are already very different, additional difference doesn't matter very much."
  # differences near zero matter a lot; differences that are already large matter progressively less.
  #smaller denominator → score falls faster → more sensitive to differences
  #larger denominator → score falls slower → less sensitive to differences
  #So the denominator defines the scale of difference that you consider substantial.

  score <- 100 * exp(
    -difference / desired_income
  )

  return(score)
}

#Numbers of working hours compatability
hours_match <- function(country_hours, desired_hours) {

  difference <- abs(country_hours - desired_hours)

  #smaller 10 → score falls faster → more sensitive to differences
  #larger 10 → score falls slower → less sensitive to differences
  #when difference = 10, your score has fallen to exactly 100e−1≈36.8.

  score <- 100 * exp(
    -difference / 10
  )

  return(score)
}

  #Update the age choices so only age groups available for the chosen
  #education level can be selected
  observeEvent(input$education, {

    available_ages <- df %>%
      filter(
        education == input$education,
        age_group != "All ages"
      ) %>%
      distinct(age_group) %>%
      pull(age_group)

    updateSelectInput(
      session,
      "age_group",
      choices = available_ages,
      selected = if (input$age_group %in% available_ages) {
        input$age_group
      } else {
        available_ages[1]
      }
    )
  })

  #Getting the user data, to get the correct reference group
  results <- reactive({

    #The wellbeing indicators are available by education at "All ages".
    #Therefore these are retrieved separately from the age-specific
    #labour market indicators.
    wellbeing_data <- df %>%
      filter(
        education == input$education,
        age_group == "All ages"
      ) %>%
      select(
        iso3,
        country,
        pct_happy,
        pct_satisfied_finances,
        pct_satisfied_leisure
      )

    #Getting age-specific work and economic data for the user's education group
    work_data <- df %>%
      filter(
        education == input$education,
        age_group == input$age_group
      ) %>%
      select(
        iso3,
        country,
        earnings_gross_yearly,
        hours_worked,
        pct_permanent_contract
      )

    #Combining the two OECD reference groups by country
    data <- wellbeing_data %>%
      inner_join(
        work_data,
        by = c("iso3", "country")
      )

    #Removing countries where one or more indicators required
    #for the score are unavailable
    data <- data %>%
      filter(
        !is.na(pct_happy),
        !is.na(pct_satisfied_finances),
        !is.na(pct_satisfied_leisure),
        !is.na(earnings_gross_yearly),
        !is.na(hours_worked),
        !is.na(pct_permanent_contract)
      )

    #Check that we have data
    validate(
      need(
        nrow(data) > 0,
        "No complete data is available for this education and age combination."
      )
    )

    #Getting the user input importance "weights"
    weights <- c(
      happiness = input$weight_happiness,
      finance = input$weight_finance,
      leisure = input$weight_leisure,
      contract = input$weight_contract,
      income = input$weight_income,
      hours = input$weight_hours
    )

    #Normalising the weights so that the sum is always 1 (100%)
    if (sum(weights) == 0) {
      weights <- rep(1, length(weights))
      names(weights) <- c(
        "happiness", "finance", "leisure",
        "contract", "income", "hours"
      )
    }

    weights <- weights / sum(weights)

    # Making the scores for the indicators, all except income and time from raw data
    # + adding the contribution facotrs from the user
    # + adding the total calculated country wellbeing score for the user
    data <- data %>%
      mutate(

        happiness_score =
          pct_happy,

        contribution_happiness =
          weights["happiness"] *
          happiness_score,

        finance_score =
          pct_satisfied_finances,

        contribution_finance =
          weights["finance"] *
          finance_score,

        leisure_score =
          pct_satisfied_leisure,

        contribution_leisure =
          weights["leisure"] *
          leisure_score,

        contract_score =
          pct_permanent_contract,

        contribution_contract =
          weights["contract"] *
          contract_score,

        income_match_score =
          income_match(
            earnings_gross_yearly,
            input$income
          ),

        contribution_income =
          weights["income"] *
          income_match_score,

        hours_match_score =
          hours_match(
            hours_worked,
            input$hours
          ),

        contribution_hours =
          weights["hours"] *
          hours_match_score,

        personalised_score =
          contribution_happiness +
          contribution_finance +
          contribution_leisure +
          contribution_contract +
          contribution_income +
          contribution_hours
      )

    #Reformatting datatable, one country per row
    #After combining the education and age reference groups there is already
    #one usable row per country, so the columns are renamed here for the outputs.
    data <- data %>%
      arrange(desc(personalised_score)) %>%
      mutate(
        rank = row_number()
      ) %>%
      transmute(
        rank = rank,
        country = country,
        iso3 = iso3,
        score = personalised_score,
        happiness = happiness_score,
        finance = finance_score,
        leisure = leisure_score,
        contract = contract_score,
        income = earnings_gross_yearly,
        hours = hours_worked,
        income_match = income_match_score,
        hours_match = hours_match_score,
        contribution_happiness = contribution_happiness,
        contribution_finance = contribution_finance,
        contribution_leisure = contribution_leisure,
        contribution_contract = contribution_contract,
        contribution_income = contribution_income,
        contribution_hours = contribution_hours
      )

    return(data)
  })

  # The results
  output$summary <- renderUI({

    best <- results() %>%
      slice(1)

    tags$div(
      class = "wellbeing-result",
      tags$h2(
        paste(
          "Your recommended country is",
          best$country
        )
      ),
      tags$p(
        paste0(
          "Personalised Country Wellbeing Score: ",
          round(best$score, 1),
          " / 100"
        )
      )
    )
  })

  # Why was that country selected for you?
  output$why_country <- renderUI({

    best <- results() %>%
      slice(1)

    contributions <- data.frame(
      factor = c(
        "Happiness",
        "Financial satisfaction",
        "Leisure satisfaction",
        "Employment security",
        "Income compatibility",
        "Working-hours compatibility"
      ),
      contribution = c(
        best$contribution_happiness,
        best$contribution_finance,
        best$contribution_leisure,
        best$contribution_contract,
        best$contribution_income,
        best$contribution_hours
      )
    ) %>%
      arrange(desc(contribution))

    top_factors <- contributions %>%
      slice_head(n = 3)

    tags$div(
      tags$p(
        paste0(
          best$country,
          " ranks first for your profile."
        )
      ),
      tags$p(
        "Its three strongest contributors are:"
      ),
      tags$ol(
        tags$li(top_factors$factor[1]),
        tags$li(top_factors$factor[2]),
        tags$li(top_factors$factor[3])
      ),
      tags$p(
        paste0(
          round(best$happiness, 1),
          "% of the relevant education group report being happy."
        )
      ),
      tags$p(
        paste0(
          "Income compatibility: ",
          round(best$income_match, 1),
          "/100. Working-hours compatibility: ",
          round(best$hours_match, 1),
          "/100."
        )
      )
    )
  })

  # Weight contribution charts for the different indicators
  output$contribution_plot <- renderPlot({

    best <- results() %>%
      slice(1)

    contribution_data <- data.frame(
      factor = c(
        "Happiness",
        "Financial satisfaction",
        "Leisure",
        "Employment security",
        "Income match",
        "Working hours"
      ),
      contribution = c(
        best$contribution_happiness,
        best$contribution_finance,
        best$contribution_leisure,
        best$contribution_contract,
        best$contribution_income,
        best$contribution_hours
      )
    )

    ggplot(
      contribution_data,
      aes(
        x = reorder(factor, contribution),
        y = contribution
      )
    ) +
      geom_col() +
      coord_flip() +
      labs(
        title = paste(
          "Why",
          best$country,
          "ranks first"
        ),
        x = NULL,
        y = "Contribution to score"
      ) +
      theme_minimal()
  })

  #Your top 10 countries table
  output$country_table <- renderTable({

    results() %>%
      slice_head(n = 10) %>%
      transmute(
        Rank = rank,
        Country = country,
        `Wellbeing Score` =
          round(score, 1),
        `Happy %` =
          round(happiness, 1),
        `Financially Satisfied %` =
          round(finance, 1),
        `Leisure Satisfied %` =
          round(leisure, 1),
        `Permanent Contract %` =
          round(contract, 1),
        `Income Match` =
          round(income_match, 1),
        `Hours Match` =
          round(hours_match, 1)
      )

  }, striped = TRUE, bordered = TRUE, spacing = "s")

  # Your top 10 countries plot
  output$country_plot <- renderPlot({

    plot_data <- results() %>%
      slice_head(n = 10)

    ggplot(
      plot_data,
      aes(
        x = reorder(country, score),
        y = score
      )
    ) +
      geom_col() +
      coord_flip() +
      labs(
        title = "Your Top 10 Country Matches",
        x = NULL,
        y = "Personalised Wellbeing Score"
      ) +
      theme_minimal()
  })
}

title: Find Your Best Match
text:
2. Preparing the numeric indicators
The indicators used in mathematical calculations are explicitly converted to numeric variables.
#Making sure data is numeric
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    pct_happy = as.numeric(pct_happy),
    pct_satisfied_finances = as.numeric(pct_satisfied_finances),
    pct_satisfied_leisure = as.numeric(pct_satisfied_leisure),
    pct_permanent_contract = as.numeric(pct_permanent_contract),
    earnings_gross_yearly = as.numeric(earnings_gross_yearly),
    hours_worked = as.numeric(hours_worked)
  )

Role in the model
The variables beginning with pct_ are already expressed as percentages in the OECD data. For example, a value of 82 in pct_happy means that 82% of the relevant group reports being happy.
The percentage variables stays on their original 0–100 scale.

title: Find Your Best Match
text:
3. Measuring income and working-hours compatibility
Income and working hours are measured in numerical values and not percentages. In this format it cannot be inserted into the same weighted score as the wellbeing indicators. Instead, the model converts the difference between observed earnings and the user’s desired earnings into a 0–100 compatibility score. The same is applied to working hours.
An exact match between observed earnings and the user’s desired income receives a compatibility score of 100. As the difference increases, the score decreases.
This means the model asks:

How closely do observed earnings in this country match the user’s preferred income level?

rather than:

Which country simply has the highest earnings?

The PCWS is designed as a personalised compatibility model. A higher income is therefore not automatically treated as better. The exponential function gives relatively greater importance to differences close to the user’s target and progressively less importance to additional differences once two values are already far apart.
For the “Working hours” the denominator 10 controls how sensitive the score is to differences in working hours. It is a modelling assumption and should be interpreted as part of the model specification.
#Making the functions for compatability
#Transforming the values so that they match the other indicators % style on a scale of 0-100

#Income compatability
income_match <- function(country_income, desired_income) {

  difference <- abs(country_income - desired_income)

  # Exponential, No difference → score of 100. Bigger difference → rapidly smaller score.
  #"Small differences are meaningful, but once two things are already very different, additional difference doesn't matter very much."
  # differences near zero matter a lot; differences that are already large matter progressively less.
  #smaller denominator → score falls faster → more sensitive to differences
  #larger denominator → score falls slower → less sensitive to differences
  #So the denominator defines the scale of difference that you consider substantial.

  score <- 100 * exp(
    -difference / desired_income
  )

  return(score)
}

#Numbers of working hours compatability
hours_match <- function(country_hours, desired_hours) {

  difference <- abs(country_hours - desired_hours)

  #smaller 10 → score falls faster → more sensitive to differences
  #larger 10 → score falls slower → less sensitive to differences
  #when difference = 10, your score has fallen to exactly 100e−1≈36.8.

  score <- 100 * exp(
    -difference / 10
  )

  return(score)
}

section: 8. Combining the two OECD reference groups
text:
8. Combining the two OECD reference groups
A central feature of the current dataset is that the wellbeing indicators and labour-market indicators are not available at exactly the same demographic level.
The wellbeing percentages are available for the selected education group across "All ages", while income, working hours and permanent-contract information are available for the selected education and age group.
The model therefore retrieves the two sets of indicators separately and combines them by country.
After the join, each country has one profile containing:

happiness for the selected education group
financial satisfaction for the selected education group
leisure satisfaction for the selected education group
age-specific earnings for the selected education group
age-specific working hours
age-specific permanent-contract prevalence

This also introduces an important methodological limitation: the final score combines indicators from related but not identical demographic aggregation levels.
#Getting the user data, to get the correct reference group

#The wellbeing indicators are available by education at "All ages".
#Therefore these are retrieved separately from the age-specific
#labour market indicators.
wellbeing_data <- df %>%
  filter(
    education == input$education,
    age_group == "All ages"
  ) %>%
  select(
    iso3,
    country,
    pct_happy,
    pct_satisfied_finances,
    pct_satisfied_leisure
  )


#Getting age-specific work and economic data for the user's education group
work_data <- df %>%
  filter(
    education == input$education,
    age_group == input$age_group
  ) %>%
  select(
    iso3,
    country,
    earnings_gross_yearly,
    hours_worked,
    pct_permanent_contract
  )


#Combining the two OECD reference groups by country
data <- wellbeing_data %>%
  inner_join(
    work_data,
    by = c("iso3", "country")
  )

9. Handling missing country observations
Some countries may still be missing one or more of the indicators required to calculate the complete score. To avoid NaN values and prevening the model from inventing or imputing observations that are not present in the OECD data only countries with complete information for all six score components remain in the ranking.
Therefore the number of countries included in the ranking may vary between user profiles.
#Removing countries where one or more indicators required
#for the score are unavailable
data <- data %>%
  drop_na(
    pct_happy,
    pct_satisfied_finances,
    pct_satisfied_leisure,
    earnings_gross_yearly,
    hours_worked,
    pct_permanent_contract
  )

section: 10. Converting the importance sliders into model weights
text:
10. Converting the importance sliders into model weights
The six slider values are first collected into a vector and then nornmalised so they always add up to 100%.
#Getting the user input importance "weights"
weights <- c(
  happiness = input$weight_happiness,
  finance = input$weight_finance,
  leisure = input$weight_leisure,
  contract = input$weight_contract,
  income = input$weight_income,
  hours = input$weight_hours
)
#Normalising the weights so that the sum is always 1 (100%)
if (sum(weights) == 0) {
  weights <- rep(1, length(weights))
}

weights <- weights / sum(weights)

title: Find Your Best Match
section: 11. Calculating the Personalised Country Wellbeing Score
text:
11. Calculating the Personalised Country Wellbeing Score
Once the country indicators and user weights are available, each component is multiplied by its corresponding weight.
The final score can be written as:
[ PCWS_c = w_HH_c + w_FF_c + w_LL_c + w_EE_c + w_II_c + w_WW_c ]
where:

(H) = happiness percentage
(F) = financial-satisfaction percentage
(L) = leisure-satisfaction percentage
(E) = permanent-contract percentage
(I) = income compatibility
(W) = working-hours compatibility
each (w) represents the user’s normalised importance weight.

All six component measures use a 0–100 scale, and the weights sum to 1. The final PCWS therefore also lies on a 0–100 scale.
The score should be interpreted as a weighted compatibility index. It represents how strongly a country’s observed profile matches the user’s demographic characteristics and stated preferences.
# Making the scores for the indicators, all except income and time from raw data
# + adding the contribution facotrs from the user
# + adding the total calculated country wellbeing score for the user
data <- data %>%
  mutate(

    happiness_score =
      pct_happy,

    contribution_happiness =
      weights["happiness"] *
      happiness_score,


    finance_score =
      pct_satisfied_finances,

    contribution_finance =
      weights["finance"] *
      finance_score,


    leisure_score =
      pct_satisfied_leisure,

    contribution_leisure =
      weights["leisure"] *
      leisure_score,


    contract_score =
      pct_permanent_contract,

    contribution_contract =
      weights["contract"] *
      contract_score,


    income_match_score =
      income_match(
        earnings_gross_yearly,
        input$income
      ),

    contribution_income =
      weights["income"] *
      income_match_score,


    hours_match_score =
      hours_match(
        hours_worked,
        input$hours
      ),

    contribution_hours =
      weights["hours"] *
      hours_match_score,


    personalised_score =
      contribution_happiness +
      contribution_finance +
      contribution_leisure +
      contribution_contract +
      contribution_income +
      contribution_hours
  )

title: Find Your Best Match
text:
12. Ranking the countries
After calculating the personalised score, the countries are ordered from highest to lowest.
#Reformatting datatable, one country per row
#After combining the education and age reference groups there is already
#one usable row per country, so the columns are renamed here for the outputs.
data <- data %>%
  arrange(desc(personalised_score)) %>%
  mutate(
    rank = row_number()
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    rank = rank,
    country = country,
    iso3 = iso3,
    score = personalised_score,
    happiness = happiness_score,
    finance = finance_score,
    leisure = leisure_score,
    contract = contract_score,
    income = earnings_gross_yearly,
    hours = hours_worked,
    income_match = income_match_score,
    hours_match = hours_match_score,
    contribution_happiness = contribution_happiness,
    contribution_finance = contribution_finance,
    contribution_leisure = contribution_leisure,
    contribution_contract = contribution_contract,
    contribution_income = contribution_income,
    contribution_hours = contribution_hours

The three largest weighted contributions are reported as the main reasons the country ranked first.

title: Scrooge McDuck
text:
Where the data come from
ReICO does not rely on a single survey sent directly to Master’s and doctorate holders. National contact points compile aggregated statistics from official sources, including labour-force and graduate surveys, population censuses, and administrative records on education, employment and taxation. The OECD processes these submissions and cross-checks them against international data sources where possible.
The target population comprises residents aged 25–64. Results are reported for Master’s and doctorate holders, with further breakdowns by age group.

title: Scrooge McDuck
text:
How we prepared the data
The downloaded indicator codes contained information about three variables:

Education level: total population, Master’s degree or doctorate
Age group: total population aged 25–64, or the groups 25–34, 35–44, 45–54 and 55–64
Measure: gross annual earnings, annual hours worked, permanent contracts, happiness, financial satisfaction or satisfaction with leisure time

To prepare the data for analysis, we decoded the OECD indicator labels, standardised country names and used the OECD observation-status metadata to resolve repeated records. We then reorganised the data so that each row represents one country, education level and age group.
The final dataset contains 375 such combinations, with the six measures arranged in separate columns.
Read the OECD ReICO methodology
Visit the OECD ReICO database






ImportantA note on interpretation



All data refer to 2022.  Income values are not always reported in a standardised currency, so direct comparisons between countries should be interpreted with caution.

title: Follow the money
text:
This is the analysis of age-related data in the OECD reICO dataset. It was used to figure out, if earnings, working hours and the rate of indefinite contracts depends on the age group, the academic degree (master vs doctorate) or on the country.
If you wish to learn, how the data was tidied and filtered for the outputs on this page, feel free to explore the code below:


Code
#We restricted the analysis to observations classified by OECD as normal values (OBS_STATUS_1 = "A"). When two normal observations were available for the same country, year and indicator, we used their arithmetic mean and flagged these cases for sensitivity analysis.

library(tidyverse)
dat <- read_csv("filtered_reICO_data.csv")
head(dat)
colnames(dat)


# Keep only age-specific variables
age_data <- dat %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(
      Indicator,
      "aged 25-34|aged 35-44|aged 45-54|aged 55-64"
    )
  )

# Keep observations classified as "Normal value"
age_normal <- age_data %>%
  filter(OBS_STATUS_1 == "A")

#Coerce duplications into a mean
age_normal_check <- age_normal %>%
  group_by(REF_AREA, `Reference area`, VAR, Indicator) %>%
  summarise(
    n_values = n(),
    value_min = min(OBS_VALUE),
    value_max = max(OBS_VALUE),
    value_mean = mean(OBS_VALUE),
    difference = value_max - value_min,
    pct_difference =
      100 * difference / value_mean,
    .groups = "drop"
  )


#Create tidy table
age_tidy <- age_normal_check %>%
  mutate(
    
    # Degree
    degree = case_when(
      str_starts(VAR, "MAS") ~ "Master",
      str_starts(VAR, "PHD") ~ "Doctorate",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    # Age group
    age_group = case_when(
      str_detect(VAR, "25_34") ~ "25-34",
      str_detect(VAR, "35_44") ~ "35-44",
      str_detect(VAR, "45_54") ~ "45-54",
      str_detect(VAR, "55_64") ~ "55-64",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    # Outcome
    outcome = case_when(
      str_detect(VAR, "EARNY") ~ "Earnings",
      str_detect(VAR, "_HW")   ~ "Annual hours",
      str_detect(VAR, "PERM")  ~ "Indefinite contract",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    # Put age groups in logical order
    age_group = factor(
      age_group,
      levels = c("25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64"),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    
    # Put degree categories in logical order
    degree = factor(
      degree,
      levels = c("Master", "Doctorate")
    ),
    
    # Flag cases where more than one normal value was averaged
    duplicate_normal = n_values > 1
  ) %>%
  
  select(
    country_code = REF_AREA,
    country = `Reference area`,
    degree,
    age_group,
    outcome,
    value = value_mean,
    duplicate_normal,
    n_normal_values = n_values,
    value_min,
    value_max,
    difference,
    pct_difference,
    VAR
  ) %>%
  
  arrange(
    country,
    degree,
    outcome,
    age_group
  )

#Check that all variables got converted and no NA values exist
age_tidy %>%
  filter(
    is.na(degree) |
    is.na(age_group) |
    is.na(outcome)
  )

#Inspect coverage
age_tidy %>%
  count(degree, outcome, age_group)

#Check that no duplicate values remain
age_tidy %>%
  count(country, degree, age_group, outcome) %>%
  filter(n > 1)








NoteNote on uneven data distribution



The analysis results are based on a survey carried out in many countries across the world. Unfortunately, the responses are very unevenly distributed between countries. You can explore this further in Table 1.



Question 1
How do earnings, working hours, and job security change with age? Are the patterns different for Master’s and Doctorate holders?
First, we need to tidy the data a bit more. If you wish to see, how this was done, follow the plot below.

#Number of countries:

#Create age-dependent change relative to 25-34 years

Does the age–earnings pattern depend on the country of residence? For this analysis, we selected countries with all datapoints available. If you wish to see, how we did this, check out the code below:


Code

  filter(
    outcome == "Earnings",

  ) %>%

    n_age_groups = n_distinct(age_group),
    .groups = "drop"

  filter(n_degrees == 2) %>%
  pull(country)


#Organize data for heatmap

  filter(
    outcome == "Earnings",
    country %in% balanced_countries
  ) %>%
  
  group_by(country, degree) %>%
  
  mutate(
    earnings_25_34 = value[age_group == "25-34"],
    
    earnings_change =
      100 * (value / earnings_25_34 - 1)
  ) %>%
  
  ungroup()

#Sort countries according to their older age earnings
country_order <- heatmap_data %>%
  filter(age_group == "55-64") %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    senior_premium = mean(earnings_change, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(senior_premium) %>%
  pull(country)

#Apply ordering
heatmap_data <- heatmap_data %>%
  mutate(
    country = factor(
      country,
      levels = country_order
    )
  )

What do the results in Figure 2 tell us?

Aging is not generally a bad thing - in all countries, people in higher age groups earn more than young people between 25-34.
However, in some countries the earnings decline in the age-group 55-64 years in comparison to people 10 years younger.



Question 3
Is it overall worth to pursue a PhD over MSc? Does it pay off at older age? Or does this depend on the country you live in?
This is how we rearranged the data:

    country,
    degree,
    age_group,
    value

  pivot_wider(
    names_from = age_group,
    values_from = value

    values_from = age_premium

People holding a doctorate degree generally earn more by the end of their career in comparison to their colleagues with master degrees.

# VAR is a structured code: "<numerator>X<denominator>" for shares, or a plain
# code for levels. The numerator encodes education, measure and age band, e.g.
#   PHD_TOC_PERM_35_44XPHD_TOC_35_44   MAS_EARNY_25_34   TOTWB_HAPPY_GESMTXTOTWB
measure_labels <- c(
  "_TOC_PERM"        = "pct_permanent_contract",
  "_HW"              = "hours_worked",
  "_EARNY"           = "earnings_gross_yearly",
  "_HAPPY_GESMT"     = "pct_happy",
  "_FINS_MEDHIGH"    = "pct_satisfied_finances",
  "_TIMEUSE_MEDHIGH" = "pct_satisfied_leisure"
)

# Observed values first, then caveated, then imputed. Q is always a missing value.
status_priority <- c("A", "B", "D", "U", "V", "I", "Q")

data_long <- data_table |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    num_code  = str_remove(VAR, "X.*$"),
    core_code = num_code |>
      str_remove("^(TOT|MAS|PHD)(WB)?") |>
      str_remove("_\\d{2}_\\d{2}$"),
    education = factor(str_extract(num_code, "^(TOT|MAS|PHD)"),
                       levels = c("TOT", "MAS", "PHD"),
                       labels = c("Total population", "Master's", "Doctorate")),
    age_group = num_code |>
      str_extract("\\d{2}_\\d{2}") |>
      str_replace("_", "-") |>
      replace_na("All ages") |>
      factor(levels = c("All ages", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64")),
    measure   = unname(measure_labels[core_code])
  )

# Fail loud if a VAR code ever stops matching the pattern above.
stopifnot(!anyNA(data_long$education), !anyNA(data_long$age_group),
          !anyNA(data_long$measure))

# 154 country x VAR pairs appear 2-3 times under different observation statuses.
# Keep the best-status rows, then average whatever is still tied.
data_long <- data_long |>
  dplyr::mutate(status_rank = match(OBS_STATUS_1, status_priority)) |>
  slice_min(status_rank, by = c(REF_AREA, VAR), with_ties = TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    value    = if (all(is.na(OBS_VALUE))) NA_real_ else mean(OBS_VALUE, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_source = n(),
    .by = c(REF_AREA, `Reference area`, VAR, Indicator,
            education, age_group, measure, `Observation status`)
  ) |>
  rename(iso3 = REF_AREA, country = `Reference area`, status = `Observation status`) |>
  arrange(country, education, age_group, measure)

# One row per country x education x age band, one column per measure.
data_wide <- data_long |>
  select(iso3, country, education, age_group, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(country, education, age_group)

# Correct the country name for Turkey since was encoded as latin1, and now back to UTF-8
data_wide <- data_wide |> dplyr::mutate(country = if_else(iso3 == "TUR", "Türkiye", country))

# The original Indicator text cannot be a column in the wide table (each row
# spans up to 6 indicators), so keep it as a lookup for axis labels / tooltips.
indicator_dict <- data_long |>
